stories.headline: Re/Max Cofounder Gail Liniger Dies at 81, Days After Company's $880 Million Sale
stories.summary:
Gail Liniger, who cofounded Denver-based Re/Max and helped build it into one of the world's largest real estate franchise networks, has died at age 81. Her death was announced just days after the company completed its $880 million sale to The Real Brokerage.

Re/Max was founded in Denver in 1973 by Gail and Dave Liniger, and grew from a local brokerage into a global brand with tens of thousands of agents operating under its distinctive red, white and blue balloon logo. The company long served as one of Denver's most prominent corporate anchors.

The timing of her death — coming immediately after the landmark sale that ended the Linigers' decades-long ownership era — marks the close of a defining chapter in Colorado business history. No additional details about the cause of death or memorial arrangements were immediately available.

stories.headline: Denver Nightclub to Reopen With New Safety Measures After Security Guard Accused of Sexual Assault
stories.summary:
Olympus Discotheque, a Denver nightclub at 2036 N. Broadway, will be allowed to reopen after reaching an agreement with city licensing officials following an emergency closure earlier this month. The closure came after an unlicensed security guard was accused of holding an 18-year-old woman at gunpoint and sexually assaulting her in an hour-long attack after the club closed on July 18.

Under the agreement, owner Wuilmer Varela Cardoza will pay a $2,000 fine and must implement a series of new safety measures. These include employing at least two licensed security guards or off-duty police officers during late-night hours, conducting pat-downs and metal detector sweeps on weekend nights, installing additional security cameras, and ensuring all customers leave by 2:15 a.m.

The club faces a doubled fine and a 60-day closure if Cardoza fails to comply with the conditions. City officials noted that summary suspensions of this kind are historically rare emergency measures, though Denver has issued three such suspensions so far this year — including one following a shooting at a southeast Denver nightclub that killed one person and wounded eight others.

stories.headline: Colorado Secretary of State's Office Exposed Confidential Voter Data for More Than 130,000 Residents
stories.summary:
The Colorado Secretary of State's Office inadvertently made information for more than 130,000 confidential voters publicly accessible for over a week due to an error introduced during a routine update to an online voter registration tool. Agency officials confirmed Thursday that 59 voter profiles for people who had specifically requested their records not be publicly disclosed were accessed between Aug. 14 and late Tuesday afternoon, when the problem was discovered.

The error occurred when staff updated the 'Find my voter registration' tool to comply with new state requirements allowing preregistered voters aged 17 and a half to check their registrations online. Department officials said they believe many, though not all, of the 59 searches were likely people accessing their own information, based on IP address analysis and follow-up conversations with affected voters.

Secretary of State Jena Griswold, the Democratic nominee for Colorado attorney general in November's election, issued an apology and said her office immediately reversed the update upon discovering the problem. The office said it will implement new automated and manual testing protocols to prevent future breaches. This is not the first such incident under Griswold's tenure; in 2024, office staff inadvertently posted online a spreadsheet containing partial passwords to parts of the state's voting systems.

stories.headline: Rep. Jeff Hurd Campaigns on Disagreements With Trump as CD-3 Reelection Race Grows Competitive
stories.summary:
U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, a Grand Junction Republican representing Colorado's 3rd Congressional District, is running an unusual reelection campaign that highlights his votes in opposition to President Donald Trump, including votes to extend Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies, override Trump's veto of a water bill affecting southeastern Colorado, and reverse Trump's tariffs on Canadian imports. Hurd told constituents at a Glenwood Springs library event that he hopes voters see him as a voice of independence willing to take unpopular stands.

The strategy sets Hurd apart from the three other Republicans in Colorado's congressional delegation, who are largely running on their alignment with the president. Hurd lost Trump's endorsement over the tariff vote, though Trump later reendorsed him in March after being persuaded Republicans could not afford to lose the seat.

Hurd's approach carries risks. Critics point to his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — the Trump-backed tax and spending legislation — as evidence of alignment with the president, and Democrats are using that vote to argue he cut Medicaid funding to benefit wealthy taxpayers. At the Glenwood Springs event, a constituent challenged Hurd directly about her family's reduced Medicaid stipend for her 45-year-old son with a developmental disability, illustrating the political vulnerabilities Hurd faces heading into November.

stories.headline: Antitrust Lawsuit Accuses Four Largest Ski Resort Companies of Operating a Pricing 'Cartel'
stories.summary:
A group of skiers has filed a lawsuit in Colorado's U.S. District Court alleging that the four largest ski resort operators — Colorado-based Vail Resorts and Alterra Mountain Co., Michigan's Boyne Resorts and Utah's Powdr — conspired to share confidential pricing information and inflate ticket and pass prices at the nation's 30 largest destination ski resorts in violation of federal antitrust law. The complaint seeks class action status on behalf of thousands of skiers who purchase lift tickets, season passes and ski lessons.

The lawsuit also names Boulder research firm RRC Associates and the Lakewood-based National Ski Areas Association, alleging the organizations served as conduits for the exchange of competitively sensitive information. The complaint argues that $350 single-day ticket prices effectively coerce skiers into purchasing $1,000 season passes, shifting the financial risk of poor snow seasons onto consumers.

This is the second such antitrust lawsuit filed this year in Colorado federal court, and a third was filed Monday by a Vail Resorts shareholder who names the company and all nine of its board members, including CEO Rob Katz. Vail Resorts has moved to dismiss the first lawsuit, arguing its season pass discounting strategy represents legitimate competition rather than an antitrust violation. Vail Resorts reported that visitation at its Western U.S. ski areas fell more than 20% last winter, the steepest annual decline in the company's history.

stories.headline: E-Bike Injuries in Children Surge 184% at Children's Hospital Colorado, Doctors Warn
stories.summary:
Children's Hospital Colorado's Anschutz Medical Campus in Aurora recorded a 184% increase in children severely injured by e-bikes between 2024 and 2025, and as of June 2026 had already documented more traumatic e-bike injuries than in all of 2025, according to hospital trauma program officials. Physicians say the injuries — which frequently include traumatic brain injuries, skull fractures, severe internal bleeding and broken bones — are not minor scrapes and often require surgery and lengthy hospital stays.

Doctors attribute the spike partly to a widespread misunderstanding of e-bike classifications. Colorado State Patrol Lt. Col. Josh Downing noted that e-bikes are legally capped at 28 mph and 750 watts, and any device exceeding those specifications — whether by design or post-purchase modification — legally requires a motorcycle license to operate. Many parents are unknowingly purchasing what amount to motorcycles for their children.

Similar trends have been observed at Children's Hospital in Colorado Springs and at other facilities statewide, according to Dr. Maria Mandt, director of emergency medical services and critical care transport at the Anschutz campus. Hospital officials are urging parents to ensure children wear helmets, understand the class of e-bike they are riding and receive appropriate supervision, emphasizing that many of the most serious injuries seen daily are preventable.

stories.headline: Jefferson County Foresters Remove 60% of Trees on 73 Acres at Lookout Mountain to Reduce Wildfire Risk
stories.summary:
Jefferson County foresters have removed approximately 60% of small and medium-sized trees — roughly 500 very small trees and 100 significant trees per acre — across 73 acres of Lookout Mountain Preserve and Nature Center as part of a proactive wildfire mitigation effort. The project left a more open forest of older, established ponderosa pines that natural resources supervisor Terry Auciello says can better withstand low-intensity ground fires and resist pine beetle infestations.

The initiative reflects lessons learned from a 2025 wildfire near Conifer, where the White Hawk Trail fire ignited within mitigated land and was contained relatively quickly because of easier firefighter access and reduced tree density. The historic 2025-26 drought has accelerated tree mortality along the I-70 corridor between Genesee and Floyd Hill, and Auciello warned that far more trees in that corridor will die before next summer.

Forestry officials say the work, while visually striking and sometimes controversial, is critical to protecting the watershed that more than half a million households rely on for drinking water. The piece notes that similar mitigation projects combining private landowner cooperation and state matching grants have proved effective in protecting communities in the foothills.

stories.headline: Avalanche Enter 2026-27 Season With Thin Roster After Trading Away Picks and Depth for Failed Cup Run
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche begin the 2026-27 NHL season carrying significant roster uncertainty after a painful offseason reshaping that followed a stunning first-round exit — a four-game sweep by the Vegas Golden Knights — despite posting the best record in the NHL during the regular season. Colorado had gone 55-16-11 in the regular season before injuries caught up with the team in the playoffs.

To make salary cap math work after an aggressive trade deadline that brought in Nazem Kadri, Brett Kulak and Nicolas Roy at the cost of two first-round picks and several other assets, the Avalanche were forced to trade or lose Valeri Nichushkin, Ross Colton, Jack Drury and Nick Blankenburg this summer. The team signed veteran Jaden Schwartz and acquired young, inexpensive depth players Zachary L'Heureux and Fedor Svechkov but enters the new season with barely $400,000 in salary cap space.

The moves leave the team heavily dependent on Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar and their supporting core, with little room for error or in-season additions. Analysts are questioning whether the Avalanche — who won the Stanley Cup in 2022 — are positioned for a championship run or due for a step back in what would be a concerning trend in the MacKinnon-Makar era.

stories.headline: Rockies Snap Seven-Game Losing Streak as Hunter Goodman Homers in Return From Injury
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies ended a seven-game losing streak with a 3-1 win over the Washington Nationals on Thursday, with Hunter Goodman homering in his return from a shoulder injury. Pitcher Mason Adams worked into the fifth inning in his major league debut.

The victory comes after the Rockies had snapped a separate franchise record losing streak on the road earlier in the week with a 13-1 rout of the Nationals. Colorado will monitor Kyle Karros's health closely in coming days following his own recent return from the injured list.

Prospects Cole Carrigg and Zac Veen continue to draw attention as the organization's future cornerstones, even as the team remains among the worst in the National League in 2026.

stories.headline: Broncos Prepare for Final Preseason Game Against Vikings as Bo Nix Draws Praise From Teammates
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos are heading into their final preseason game against the Minnesota Vikings following a week of training camp that included a USAA-sponsored military appreciation event at Broncos Park. Quarterback Bo Nix, entering his third year in the league, has continued to draw high praise from teammates and coaches as the regular season approaches.

Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph has been studying opposing teams' tendencies on first down, identifying patterns that opposing offenses use to neutralize Denver's pass rush. Meanwhile, cornerback Riley Moss is expected to be available after a rib injury was characterized as not serious by head coach Sean Payton, and receivers Wattenberg and Mims have returned to practice.

The Broncos' preseason camp has generated optimism heading into the 2026 regular season, with the team looking to build on improvements made during Nix's first two years under center in Denver.

stories.headline: Pueblo's Leonardo da Vinci Museum Seeks $885,000 in Taxpayer Funding, Sparking Heated City Council Debate
stories.summary:
The Pueblo City Council voted 5-2 Monday to delay action until Sept. 14 on an ordinance that would allocate $885,000 in sales tax funding to the city's Leonardo da Vinci Museum of North America, located on the Historic Arkansas Riverwalk. The delay followed an initial request for $1.8 million — later scaled back to exclude employee wages — and came after a local businesswoman publicly challenged the legality of the proposed ordinance.

Mayor Heather Graham, a strong champion of the museum, angrily rebuked council members who said they needed more information before voting, arguing that the process had been underway since April and that council members had attended multiple executive sessions on the topic. Council member Selena Ruiz-Gomez called for a point of order to stop Graham mid-statement.

Museum founder and board president Joe Arrigo, who was not present at the two closed-door work sessions where the request was discussed, addressed the council Monday along with roughly 20 supporters, mostly museum employees and volunteers. A work session has been scheduled for Sept. 8 to more thoroughly examine the museum's finances and budget projections before the council votes.

stories.headline: Hearth Bakery Opens European-Style Patisserie in Denver's West Highland Neighborhood
stories.summary:
Denver's Hearth Bakery has opened Hearth Patisserie, a European-style pastry shop, next door to its existing location at 3621 W. 32nd Ave. in the West Highland neighborhood. The new concept occupies the former Happy Cakes space and is led by pastry chef Kevin McCormick, who previously served as culinary director at Denver's Union Station and brings two decades of pastry experience.

The patisserie is focused on afternoon and evening desserts, with a seasonally rotating menu that includes entremets, tarts, choux pastry, Paris-Brest, Parisian flans, tiramisu and a tea-focused beverage program. The opening menu features items such as a reimagined cream puff in raspberry and tropical flavors, strawberry tarts with almond and mascarpone cream, and raspberry pistachio gâteaux.

Hearth was founded in 2022 and now operates four locations across Denver. The new patisserie represents an expansion of the brand's offerings beyond its established artisan sourdough, croissants and coffee into more refined dessert territory.

topStory.headline: Six Months Into Iran War, Stalemate Deepens as Hormuz Shipping Remains Severely Disrupted
topStory.summary:
The United States and Israel marked six months Friday since launching joint military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, with the conflict having evolved into a prolonged standoff that analysts say shows no signs of near-term resolution. What the Trump administration initially projected as a weeks-long campaign has produced neither Iran's surrender nor the restoration of normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints.

Approximately 6,000 sailors aboard 400 ships remain stranded in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the United Nations' International Maritime Organization reported Friday. IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said a large-scale evacuation effort has stalled — only 136 vessels and roughly 2,900 seafarers have been evacuated, with no successful extractions since late June when renewed fighting paused the operation. At least 19 mariners have been killed in the region since the war began.

U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in a video statement Thursday that the military had cleared Iranian sea mines from internationally recognized transit routes in the strait, declaring the lanes "open" with "momentum building." President Trump echoed that claim, citing the safe passage of 24 oil tankers the previous night. However, U.S. allies have disputed whether the strait has been fully de-mined, and the figure of 24 transits compares starkly with the roughly 120 ships that passed through daily before the war began.

Global markets have absorbed much of the disruption, with front-month Brent crude oil futures up nearly 20% since the war started, though well below their April peak of $126.41 per barrel. Equity markets have largely shrugged off the conflict, buoyed by corporate earnings optimism. The White House has shifted strategy toward an economic pressure campaign it has labeled "Economic D-Day," targeting Iran and its trading partners through secondary sanctions, though analysts at Eurasia Group and the Center for Strategic and International Studies said the approach is unlikely to compel Iranian capitulation, given Tehran's historical resilience under economic pressure.

Geopolitical analysts said neither side appears ready to escalate significantly or make meaningful concessions, leaving the conflict in an indefinite holding pattern. Iran has not agreed to any of the five objectives the Trump administration set out at the war's start, peace talks have collapsed, and questions remain about whether the U.S. will extend sanctions pressure to China, one of Iran's largest trading partners. A White House official told CNBC the U.S. is now "entering the endgame" of the conflict, though analysts cautioned that a breakthrough does not appear imminent.
